newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-FRENCH COURT EXPLORES SOCCER TRANSFER JUNGLE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FRENCH COURT EXPLORES SOCCER TRANSFER JUNGLE.

text.p: A French court explored the financial jungle of soccer transfers on Thursday and was told payments were inflated either to win over star players' relatives, or pay PR companies or by under-the-table dealings.
The court is trying ex-tycoon Bernard Tapie and 19 other soccer figures over the disapppearance of 100 million francs ($17 million) from the accounts of former European champions Marseille.

Portuguese intermediary Miguel Barbosa told the court he received 4.2 million francs ($720,000) for the transfer of Brazilian Jose Carlos Mozer to Marseille from Lisbon's Benfica, instead of the agreed two-million-franc ($340,000) commission, because he ensured an "after-sale service."

"I get the players out of their favelas (slums), I look after their families, I make sure they feel good...I must be near them. I am almost a father to them," said Barbosa, who has a virtual monopoly on transfers of Brazilian players and is dubbed the world's most expensive soccer intermediary.
Tapie's former right-hand man Jean-Pierre Bernes said the sum had been inflated in order to conceal previous illegal payments by Marseille and Barbosa had signed the contract later.
Barbosa faces charges of falsification and being an accomplice to fraud and misuse of corporate funds.

Bernes, who faces similar charges, said Marseille had paid 300,000 francs ($50,000) over the agreed 500,000 ($86,000) for Senegalese Pape Fall because "transfers from Africa are special. You have to give money to the family, the club."
Asked why the extra money never showed up in the accounts, Bernes said: "There was something wrong, as often happens in soccer circles."
Tapie passed the buck, saying he had not been aware of the extra payment and his job as chairman was not to check that the payment matched the contract.

Marseille's ex-sporting director Michel Hidalgo, France's former national coach, said Pape may have put up the price after the contract was signed. "We wanted that player and an extra 300,000 francs would not have stopped us," he said.

Bernes angrily sparred with the ex-chairman of Mulhouse, Andre Goerig, over the transfer of Abedi Pele in which 800,000 francs ($138,000) earmarked for the Ghanaian player's public relations manager found their way into Goerig's account.
Goerig, who faces charges of falsification and being an accomplice to fraud, admitted he pocketed the money.
"I had to repay myself for under-the-table advances I had made to secure Pele's services," he told the court.
Tapie and Hidalgo said they had not been aware the extra payment was destined to Goerig.
"We never agreed to thicken the sauce to fatten up a manager. In this case, it was apparently done," Tapie said.

Tapie, who is currently serving an eight-month sentence for rigging a league game in 1993, had admitted on Wednesday breaking the law with huge fictitious loans to star players which turned out to be tax-free payments.
The trial is expected to last three weeks.
